How to get better at an instrument?
I bet there are some great tutorial videos on youtube you could watch and play along with in place of lessons. It's better than nothing.

How much do you already know about piano? An easy way to learn is via lead sheets, as long as you have a good idea what the chords and scales are. The sheet music is just the overall melody of the song/piece, with chords written above. For example, a "C" would be above a measure that needs a C chord - you choose if you want to play melodic or harmonic (pro-tip: if you can't find lead sheets for a song, go to ultimate-guitar-tabs.com and you'll find something similar - I do this for Zeppelin songs).

Musescore is a good place to check out for original pieces as well as video game scores and interesting sheet music if you're bored. It's all free, and you can listen to it before you download the sheet music. That site also lets you compose your own stuff for nearly any instrument for free.

Otherwise, just keep practicing, always trying out something just a little out of your comfort zone. It's frustrating with some of the more difficult pieces, but don't give up, because when it finally clicks, it's like a nice little adrenaline rush.

I'm wondering if by just playing easy songs and playing harder ones progressively will help me learn piano again?

Yes, that's pretty much all there is to it. Also, don't be afraid to just plunk around and use the instrument as a toy.

Self-teaching is often the most efficient way to go. A lot of the time lessons or instructional videos and books introduce a ton of wasted time. (unless you find a really top notch teacher) You'll end up spending 70% of your time trying to translate what they are saying into something that makes sense to you, waiting for them to finish demonstrating something you already understand, etc. etc. You want to maximize your playing time. A lot of beginning stuff is common sense. Also, if you learn things intuitively a) it will be more fun and engaging and activate your brain more fully and b) the benefits are compounding and will make the learning curve accelerate (e.g. if you can intuitively figure out your own fingerings, say, or recognize chord structures that you haven't been taught formally, these will all get built into your automatic systems and make learning things in the future less of a grind because you have an innate understanding of what you are doing). Practicing should feel like meditating. There is always something to learn from what you are doing in the moment, don't grind through some exercise; allow yourself to stop and examine something if it catches your attention.

i've been learning piano on my own for two years now (started late too, but just like you was forced 2-3 months as kid), here are my TL;DR findings going about the hard route, mostly useful for jazz i guess:

As early as possible you want to learn your 11 majors scales, use a metronome, start slow and speed up. Learning the scales is not just learning the sequence but also its diatonic chords in all inversions (limit to 4 notes chords, try to get rid of the 5th, also try to spread the notes in your two hands, don't just do stacking). This shit needs to become second nature. Use 2-5-1 progressions as well when learning the chords (in fact go around the circle of fifth), might as well pick up the most common progression ever at the same time. Once you know all 11 major keys, congrats, you have also learned the 11 minor keys for they use the same notes, start your C scale from A to A, you play an A minor scale, beauty, and you have got the chords down too. There are more but that alone covers 99.99% of music (note that there are alternative minor scales with alterations though).

A lot of work also happens away from the piano, you need to listen to a lot of what you want to end up playing, over and over and over, know it by heart, start by following the roots, then hear every single notes even in the harmony (sing all them tones if it's hard, i find i can do it even if i have a hard time singling out the tones in my ears). You need this ability to poly-hear for the piano. My virtual teacher is Erroll Garner as he is the one who made me want to learn, it ain't easy, i still can't pick out everything he is doing, but I'd say i started hearing maybe 40% of what he was doing and now i'd say i hear a good 95% (and can only play like 40% of it still haha, nothing to be ashamed of i think considering it's late self training, also incidentally i can play a metric shit ton of simpler music now, which goes to your point i think)

Then hand independence... imo there are two layers, a huge amount of music can be played with the first layer which is not true hand independence in the sense that there is only one track in your brain and you just trained your hands to shared it, it's relatively easy to achieve. But then if you want to go higher (poly rhythm and improv for example, although some of that can be played in first layer), you need the second layer (which I'm barely touching at this point), two tracks in your head, one for each hand. The best thing i found to train this so far is Bach's counter point, just listening to it makes you progress, but of course it'll be a lot of practice on the instrument.

For improv, you just need to go at it the way babies go about language, trial and error, start slow, sing what you want to play, don't let your hands dictate the music, dictate it to your hands by singing, you will make mistakes but that's ok, start slow, as you get comfortable, speed up. Use a metronome, train both hands.

At least 20 mins per day, weekends allowed otherwise, also close your eyes every now and then, eventually it'll work and it'll blow your mind. METRONOME is mandatory though, you need that shit regardless of how hard you think you don't.

If you have questions shoot, otherwise good luck!
